At the height of Trump's trade war with China, with tariffs being raised almost weekly, companies like Logitech promptly raised the prices of their products in the US significantly.

Earlier this year, the US Supreme Court ruled these tariffs illegal and ordered refunds to manufacturers. However, no company has yet been seen passing on the refunds to consumers, and a class action lawsuit is now underway to try to correct this...

The background to the Trump tariff saga

Last year, Trump seized on the US trade deficit with China, apparently fantasising that slapping hefty tariffs on Chinese-made products would force companies like Apple to move their production lines back to the US.

Of course, that was never going to happen. The US lacks the manufacturing infrastructure, expertise and cheap labour needed to make consumer electronics at the scale required by major brands.

Trump kept claiming China would pay the tariffs, but in reality the costs were borne by US brands importing finished goods, who passed the increased costs on to consumers in the form of higher prices. At the most chaotic point, tariffs hit 145%.

Take Logitech, for example, which raised prices on about half of its products by up to 25%.

Consumers deserve a refund

The US Supreme Court ultimately ruled that Trump had no authority to impose these tariffs unilaterally, and said that money already paid by US businesses must be returned, with that process now underway.

The problem is that the costs were effectively paid by consumers through higher prices, yet none of the affected companies have been seen planning to refund their customers.

Law firm CPM has filed a class action lawsuit against Logitech on behalf of consumers who paid the higher prices while the tariffs were in effect.

9to5Mac's take

There's no question about this in principle. Companies paid the tariffs, passed the extra cost on to consumers, and now the government is refunding the companies. From a moral standpoint, the companies ought to refund the corresponding portion of the purchase price to consumers who bought products during that period.

In practice, though, it would likely be extremely difficult. Logitech would need to identify all transactions made through its vast network of third-party retailers, track what buyers paid, and calculate what proportion of that was due to tariffs.

If this lawsuit ultimately succeeds, it could set a very interesting precedent — but we have to point out that in class action lawsuits, the main beneficiaries are usually the lawyers, and the average payout to consumers is typically very small.
